entries.title: Sophia Towne stars as Nazareth wins first IHSA Class 4A state championship: 'She just won't lose'
entries.summary: <p>On Nazareth’s first possession after halftime, Roadrunners junior guard Sophia Towne caught the ball on the left side of the court with her feet firmly on the IHSA logo.</p><p>As soon as the ball hit Towne’s fingertips, she immediately went into her shooting motion and knocked down a three. Towne was in complete control on Saturday with her scoring and passing. She manipulated the defense to her liking on Saturday. Her ability to draw in a defense to open up a passing window for her teammates is particularly impressive.</p><p>She plays with a flair that elicits audible reactions from the crowds. And when her shots are falling, or her teammates are thriving, there's always a wide grin on her face.</p><p>Towne had a lot to smile about after her Roadrunners were dominant in their 55-23 IHSA Class 4A state championship win over Loyola. It's the Roadrunners' first 4A state championship — they're a 3A school.</p><p>Towne told her coach, Ed Stritzel, that they weren’t losing, and she fulfilled her promise with a 17-point, five-assist performance that powered Nazareth.</p><p>“We've been waiting all year for this,” Towne said. “We were so close [last season], so we always just [being in the state championship] in the back of our minds. ‘Peak in March’ is what we always say, and once the time came, we all knew we were not losing this game.”</p><p>Nazareth star forward Stella Sakalas drew the headlines all season, but she was plagued by foul trouble all night. Stritzel has been adamant that the Roadrunners are more than a one-woman team, and it showed in the biggest game of the season.</p><p>Freshman standout Mia Gage finished with 11 points, five rebounds and five steals. Junior forward Sam Austin scored seven points and grabbed 10 rebounds. Senior guard Lyla Shelton added eight points.</p><p>Loyola had no answer for Towne off the dribble. She’s a confident player who only needs a sliver of daylight to knock down a shot. After Sakalas drew her third foul with 3:58 left in the first half, Towne continued to lead the charge.</p><p>“She just won’t lose,” Stritzel said. “[All day], she was like, ‘We’re bringing this home.’”</p><p>Sakalas is one of the best players in the state and has proved it all season. Her getting into foul trouble would be a death sentence for most teams, but not for the Roadrunners. Not only did they maintain the lead, they added to it. They didn’t falter or waver; instead, they asserted their dominance. instead they asserted their dominance.</p><p>“Loyola is a really good team, but I think we showed everybody in the state that we're the best team in Illinois,” Stritzel said.</p><p>Whether it was Gage picking off passes and going coast-to-coast, Towne knocking down deep threes and assisting her teammates, or junior forward Sam Austin being a force on the glass, Nazareth (34-3) had many contributors in the wire-to-wire win.</p><p>After allowing 11 points to Loyola in the first quarter, the Roadrunners held the Ramblers to two, four and six points in the second, third and fourth quarters. Gage led the charge in holding Loyola to its lowest scoring output of the season with her defensive activity.</p><p>“I wanted this for my seniors so bad ... just as bad as they wanted it,” Gage said.</p><p>With a 4A title win under their belts, the Roadrunners aren’t going anywhere with Towne, Austin and Gage returning next season.</p><p>“The second half of the season prepared us for these moments,” Towne said. “When the time comes, if you want to win, you want to win."<br></p>
entries.author: Kyle Williams

entries.title: White Sox' Grant Taylor pleased with his start, although he's more of a finisher
entries.summary: <p>PEORIA, Ariz. — Grant Taylor twirled the opening inning of Saturday’s game against the Mariners and said he walked away feeling pretty good about himself.</p><p>“I feel great. I feel amazing,” he said after allowing a hit and facing four hitters. “My body is in a really good spot. I’ve done a lot of work with the pitching coaches and the staff since I got here.”</p><p>Taylor is one of the Sox’ back-end relievers, but he also opened a few games last year. Both are roles Taylor said he’s comfortable with.</p><p>“I’m used to it,” he said. “I’ve thrown late in some games during the spring. I haven’t seen a lot of big league guys, so it was nice to face some guys I’ll probably see during the season.”</p><p>During the 2025 season with the Sox, Taylor started twice and finished 10 games, saving six. With as many starting arms in camp this spring, the need for an opener could decrease. Last season, when he started twice, Taylor pitched only the first inning in each outing.</p><p>“We have a lot of really good options this year,” Taylor, 23, said. “We’ll see how that shakes out.”</p><p>Saturday’s start was to simulate both an inning early and an inning late a game.</p><p>“I’m not in on those meetings of what actually the focus was,” Taylor said.</p><h3><b>More cuts</b></h3><p>The Sox made two more camp cuts on Saturday before their game against the Mariners at the Peoria Sports Complex.</p><p>They optioned right-hander Tanner McDougal to Triple-A Charlotte and assigned left-hander Noah Schultz to minor-league camp. With these moves, they have 55 players remaining in camp: 28 pitchers, five catchers, 11 infielders and 11 outfielders.</p><p>“It’s that time of camp where guys have to get their work in,” Sox manager Will Venable said. “Those guys were outstanding. They both did a great job. We talked earlier in camp about using this as a foundation for a healthy and productive season, and they did a great job doing that.”</p><p>McDougal and Schultz combined to pitch 5.1 scoreless innings against the D-backs on Thursday at Salt River Fields. McDougal threw three innings, allowed two hits and struck out two. Schultz followed with 2.1 hitless innings, also recording two strikeouts.</p><p>“We saw what they did on the mound,” Venable said. “For two young guys to be out there and have that presence and the feel for the zone with their pitches was great to see.”</p><h3><b>Drew Thorpe update</b></h3><p>The right-hander said he weathered Friday’s second throwing session off the mound much better than his first one earlier in week. The next day following the first one, he said he suffered some soreness. Not so this time.</p><p>“It feels much better,” he said on Saturday.</p><p>Thorpe underwent Tommy John ligament replacement surgery last April and is in a slow progression to return within 12 to 18 months of the procedure.</p><h3><b>Sox 5, Mariners 1</b></h3><p><b>Davis Martin </b>pitched a nifty three innings of scoreless one-hit, four-strikeout ball following Grant Taylor’s pretty clean first. Martin also walked one. Martin, who’s certainly in line for maanger Max Venable’s starting rotation, threw 50 pitches.</p><p>“I just got back into the groove a little bit,” Martin said. “It’s just going out there and competing. Don’t make it any more than it is. Yeah, I had a lot of fun.”</p><p>This was his third outing this spring, but his first in relief after the opener.</p><p><b>Andrew Benintendi </b>started on Saturday for the second time this week after recovering from a sore right side. He went 2-for-4 with two RBI singles. Prior to the game, he said he was feeling good with no lingering effects from the injury which kept him out during the first couple of weeks of March.</p><p><b>Luisangel Acuna</b> also started at second base and made a couple of nice plays. He was 0-for-3.</p><p><b>On deck</b>: Royals at Sox, 3:05 p.m. Sunday, Glendale, 1000-AM, <b>Noah Cameron</b> vs. <b>Chris Murphy</b>.<br></p>

entries.title: White Sox might be former top prospect Jarred Kelenic's final stand
entries.summary: <p>PEORIA, Ariz. — It’s safe to say Jarred Kelenic is seeking some redemption. The No. 6 pick overall by the Mets in the 2018 draft, Kelenic had all the credentials such a lofty selection granted.</p><p>He was traded to Seattle that offseason where it certainly didn’t happen, even as the top prospect in the Mariners' organization and fourth overall in Major League Baseball.</p><p>But he had played so poorly that in mid-2023 he fractured his left foot kicking a Gatorade cooler in the home dugout out of frustration. It was then on to Atlanta where it didn’t happen, either.</p><p>He’s a .211 hitter with a .658 OPS and an 84 OPS+ — well below the major-league average of 100 – for his first five seasons. He hit .167 for the Braves last year in 60 games with an OPS+ of 49. That all speaks for itself.</p><p>The White Sox might be his final stand. Kelenic is in camp on a minor league contract and doesn’t have a spot on the club’s 40-man roster. He has to make the team. How has he weathered all the ups and downs — mostly downs?</p><p>“The game is hard,” Kelenic said. “The game sucks sometimes, man. It’ll beat you down. But at the end of the day, you’ve just got to stick to your strengths and superpowers, ride with those and have as much confidence as you can in yourself in a game where you’re set up to fail.”</p><p>Kelenic is trying, but the more things change the more they remain the same. Despite his first spring homer for the Sox on Friday — a three-run shot against the Arizona Diamondbacks at Salt River Fields — the left-handed hitting outfielder is still struggling offensively below his career clip: a .200/.238/.400 slash line with seven strikeouts in 21 plate appearances.</p><p>“It’s a small sample size. It’s Arizona,” Sox manager Will Venable said. “We’re not putting any stock into this statistically. Are you hitting the ball hard? Are you playing well defensively? Are you putting in the work? And on all that he is.”</p><p>Yet, The odds are long of him making it if Kelenic doesn’t put up some significant numbers that pop open the right eyes.</p><p>“There’s a path for him. He’s still here,” Venable added. “We haven’t made any decisions yet about him or anybody else. He still has a shot.”</p><p>At 26, the time may be coming for a career change. He was one of the highest drafted players ever from the state of Wisconsin, despite never playing ball for his Waukesha West High School team. He trained through the winter instead and decided to turn down a scholarship to play college ball at the University of Louisville after he was drafted by the Mets.</p><p>It’s been a long downhill slog ever since.</p><p>“I think just like anyone has throughout life there were a lot of things I went through that were negative,” Kelenic said. “I felt like there were really big learning opportunities for me that ultimately made me who I am today just like from an approach standpoint. The outlook of who I am, my own self.</p><p>“I can’t generalize it into one thing, but I’ve just been trying to take those times that weren’t so great and turn them into a learning opportunity because that’s the only way you can get any better.”</p><p>The Mets traded him to Seattle on Dec. 3, 2018, in the seven-player deal that netted New York aging second baseman Robinson Cano and closer Edwin Diaz. He never played a day for the Mets in the major leagues, but the Mariners were jazzed to get Kelenic. It never panned out. He batted .168 with 167 strikeouts in 147 games hose first two season, 2021 and 2022.</p><p>But perhaps there will be a new dawn for him at Camelback Ranch. Kelenic drew in a deep breath and released it when asked how he’s feeling now.</p><p>“I mean, I’m feeling pretty confident,” he said. “I’m feeling really good about where my head is at and where my swing is at. Again, it’s really early. I still need some reps to keep working on some things. There’s still some pitches I’m missing that when I’m on a roll I’m mashing those things.”</p><p>He once was the top prospect in baseball. Now, Kelenic knows better than anyone else he’s on the clock.<br></p>

entries.title: Mourners honor Rev. Jesse Jackson at final funeral service: 'I love you, neighbor'
entries.summary: <p>Mourners of the Rev. Jesse Jackson gave a final goodbye to the civil rights icon for the final time before he was laid to rest Saturday, with a somber yet uplifting culmination of weeks of ceremonies that captivated thousands throughout Chicago and across the world. </p><p>Jackson, who died Feb. 16 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/morning-edition/2026/02/17/jesse-jackson-clean-slate-act-pritzker-chicago-public-schools-preckwinkle" >at age 84</a>, was remembered as a constant, global beam of hope for justice, one that lives on through his family and his organization, the Rainbow PUSH Coalition, which hosted Saturday’s private funeral service at its Kenwood headquarters, 930 E. 50th St.</p><p>“He wanted to make sure that the world he was leaving would be better than the world he was born into,” his son U.S. Rep. Jonathan Jackson said during a rousing speech. “I want the world to know that my father believed in love, he believed in dignity of all human beings and he believed that just because you were born in the slums, the slums were never born in you.”</p><p>Jackson was interred later Saturday at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/03/05/rev-jesse-jackson-laid-rest-oak-woods-cemetery" >Oak Woods Cemetery</a>, 1035 E. 67th St.</p><p>Among Jackson’s many famed sentiments was his emphasis on understanding a person’s roots. “It’s not about where you are, but where you come from,” he’d say.</p><p>His youngest daughter, Ashley Jackson, recalled a road trip her father took her on when she was 15. He showed her <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/03/02/the-rev-jesse-jackson-greenville-south-carolina-colombia-greenville8-lying-in-state-chicago" >his childhood home in Greenville, South Carolina</a>, and sites that formed his roots in the South, like Selma, Alabama, where he first met Martin Luther King Jr.</p><p>“He wasn’t simply showing me a house. He was teaching me something about beginnings,” Ashley Jackson said. “That even when they are shadowed, they still hold light. That the distance between where you start and where you stand is sacred ground. And that what you build in that distance becomes your character.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> <bsp-carousel class="Carousel Enhancement" the chapel’s pews, which at times glowed a sunlit orange through the colorful stained glass windows.</p><p>An energetic crowd at one point shouted, “Keep hope alive,” a nod to Jackson’s famous speech <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/02/17/rev-jesse-jackson-legacy-chicago-democrats" >at the 1988 Democratic National Convention</a>. Other speakers hinted at the divisiveness in the U.S. under the Trump administrations.</p><p>Pop icon Stevie Wonder drew countless camera flashes as he performed “As,” and “They Won’t Go When I Go,” a song which he said reminded him of a time he marched with Jackson in Connecticut.</p><p>Wonder also performed a short version of the gospel song “We Shall Overcome,” an anthem of the Civil Rights Movement.</p><p>“Since I was 13, 14 years old, I’ve heard that song and I thought it was ‘we’ who should overcome,” Wonder said. “But today, it is not we who need to overcome. It is you — and you know who you are. You need to overcome hate, you need to overcome the mindset of white supremacy.”</p><p>“You shall overcome the need to dominate every single country and every people,” Wonder said. “You need to overcome gun violence, gang violence, cartel violence, government violence and domestic violence, and then this nation needs to overcome whatever fear that keeps us protecting child traffickers. Children must be protected across party lines. The innocent knows no politics.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-1a0000" name="image-1a0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/25d91c2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5787x3248+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7c%2Fc3%2F290d88fd4e859bb0f1c6fbb69b6b%2Fjackson-030826-31.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/16dad38/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5787x3248+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7c%2Fc3%2F290d88fd4e859bb0f1c6fbb69b6b%2Fjackson-030826-31.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5aad309/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5787x3248+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7c%2Fc3%2F290d88fd4e859bb0f1c6fbb69b6b%2Fjackson-030826-31.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Stevie Wonder performs during the final homegoing service for Rev. Jesse Jackson at Rainbow PUSH Coalition headquarters.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Comedian Chris Tucker kept the room in high spirits with a short speech about meeting Jackson when they coincidentally ended up on the same plane while traveling to a funeral. </p><p>“The Rev. told me some wisdom I’ll never forget," Tucker recalled. "He said, ‘Chris, the thing about flying like this so much, you miss the details, you miss the details.’ And I realized how much he sacrificed and gave to so many people and came and supported his people, for his people and other people and the world. He missed so much and he worked so hard,” said Tucker, who said he was forever grateful to Jackson for visiting his mother in the hospital when she dealt with a serious illness.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/03/06/rev-jesse-jackson-chicago-service-house-of-hope-pullman-neighborhood-barack-obama-jb-pritzker" >Chicago comes out in force to honor Rev. Jesse Jackson</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Jackson’s social and political impacts are well documented, but his reach was personal for Randi Johnson. “I came out today because Rev. Jesse Jackson is the reason I went to college," she said. </p><p>At 13, Johnson met Jackson for the first time at one of Rainbow PUSH’s college tours. She said she fell in love with his alma mater of North Carolina A&T and decided to get a higher education degree, eventually graduating from Lane College in Tennessee.</p><p>Sheila Clay, a 77-year-old artist, said she had many encounters with Jackson, from phone calls with him to going to New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina with him, to marching down Michigan Avenue with him. What stood out to Clay was how much he showed “divine love for his neighbor," she said. </p><p>“It touched my heart, because you don’t often hear many people just say, ‘I love you, neighbor.’”</p><p>Clay said Jackson’s fight for justice and love — which she first learned of at the age of 16 when her uncle told her about Operation Breadbasket — has always inspired her life and art.</p><p>“It wouldn’t be right not to come to say goodbye for the last time to my beautiful spirit, my Rev. Jesse Jackson,” Clay said. </p>

entries.title: Cubs get kick out of Japanese fan favorite Seiya Suzuki in WBC
entries.summary: <p>MESA, Ariz. — Cubs players received an added feature during their meeting before their morning workout Saturday.</p><p>They were treated to a video clip — provided by former major-league outfielder <b>Adam Jones</b> — from the outfield of the Tokyo Dome, where fans chanted the name of Cubs outfielder <b>Seiya Suzuki</b> moments before he hit one of his two home runs to lead Japan to an 8-6 victory against Korea in the World Baseball Classic.</p><p>‘‘The place goes crazy, and everybody’s hugging each other. Really cool,’’ said manager <b>Craig Counsell</b>, who got the video from Jones. ‘‘It must have been . . . a great experience, and that’s why you play the WBC — for moments like that.</p><p>‘‘These are different experiences, and this is just a life experience. And all the experiences, they mean something to you. But I think you want experiences like that.’’</p><p>Suzuki is making up for lost time since missing the 2023 WBC because of an oblique injury. He’s 3-for-7 with four runs scored in two games for Japan.</p><p>‘‘He’s been phenomenal,’’ Cubs left-hander and countryman <b>Shota Imanaga</b> said.</p><h3>No guarantees for Assad</h3><p>Right-hander <b>Javier Assad</b> pitched 3 2/3 scoreless innings in Mexico’s WBC victory Friday against Great Britain, six days after he pitched three scoreless innings and struck out four against the Dodgers.</p><p>Counsell pointed out the WBC, which is played during spring training at a high level, forces performers to prepare sooner than during a regular spring.</p><p>Assad has shown flashes of strong play during the last two seasons with the Cubs, only to be sidelined because of injuries to his right forearm and oblique. His development is valuable to the Cubs, who also are grooming right-handers <b>Colin Rea</b> and <b>Ben Brown</b> in emergency-starter roles in case of an injury to a member of their rotation.</p><p>But there’s plenty to assess entering the final 2½ weeks of spring training.</p><p>‘‘With somebody like Javy, you don’t try to figure out where they fit,’’ Counsell said. ‘‘We don’t have to do that. At some point, we’re gonna need Javy’s outs. When is probably the question.</p><p>‘‘But we want him pitching well and showing the ability to get big-league hitters out at a pretty high level. In 2024, for a couple of months, he was really one of the better starters going. You take note of things like that, and we’ve got a good version of what Javy looks like right now, the way he’s throwing the ball.’’</p><h3>Pause button on ABS success rate</h3><p>The Cubs and White Sox are at least two of several teams in the majors that have examined data in the minors in preparation for the automated ball/strike challenge system that will be implemented in the big leagues this season.</p><p>Catcher <b>Moises Ballesteros</b> has been successful on his last seven challenges, including four Wednesday against the Brewers.</p><p>But Counsell told reporters Ballesteros’ success rate of challenging pitch calls was around 50% while catching in Triple-A, where the ABS system has been used for the last couple of seasons.</p><p>‘‘It’s actually below the catchers’ average,’’ Counsell said. ‘‘My point is, I think you guys are going to say, ‘He’s good at this,’ or, ‘He’s good at that.’ And I just think we’re going to revert to the mean in this thing very quickly.’’</p><p>But is it safe to say Ballesteros, who is projected to be the Cubs’ designated hitter and third catcher, showed confidence in challenging calls?</p><p>‘‘Yeah, that’s a good point,’’ Counsell said. ‘‘I like that.’’</p><h3>Cubs 4, Athletics 3</h3><p>Left-hander <b>Shota Imanaga</b> worked exclusively on his location and was one out away from retiring his ninth consecutive batter before <b>Andy Ibanez</b> hit a high fly that eluded <b>Ian Happ</b> against the left-field fence for a double. Two batters later, <b>Brian Serven</b> clubbed a two-run home run to center. Imanaga yielded three runs and five hits in his 3 2/3-inning stint, but he didn’t walk a batter. His fastball was clocked in the 92 to 93 mph range.</p><p>• <b>Nico Hoerner</b> showed why he’s the Cubs’ most unselfish hitter and one of the most clutch hitters in the National League. He poked a two-out single down the right-field line to score <b>Josiah Hartshorn</b> and cap a two-run rally in the second.</p><p>• Infielder <b>Pedro Ramirez</b> was presented with his 2025 minor-league Gold Glove Award in a pregame ceremony, then smacked a homer to left-center against <b>Mason Barnett</b> in the second.</p><p>• <b>On deck:</b> Giants at Cubs, 3:05 p.m. Sunday, Mesa, Marquee, 104.3-FM, TBA vs. <b>Hunter Harvey</b>.<br></p>

entries.title: Fire play to 0-0 draw against Crew
entries.summary: <p>COLUMBUS, Ohio — Chris Brady finished with three saves for the Chicago Fire and Patrick Schulte stopped two shots for Columbus as the longtime rivals played to a scoreless draw in the Crew's home opener on Saturday night.</p><p>It was the 24th draw in the 80th meeting between the two clubs with the victories knotted at 28 apiece.</p><p>Five yellow cards were handed out in the final 13 minutes of regulation — three of them to the Fire (1-1-1).</p><p>Brady had two saves and Schulte wasn’t tested in the first half.</p><p>The two clubs split a pair of matches last season with both winning at home.</p><p>Columbus falls to 0-1-2 on the season.</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>Chicago: Hosts D.C. United on Saturday.</p><p>Columbus: Hosts Nashville SC on Saturday.<br></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Kind gesture blows up in an unpredictable fashion
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Eighteen months ago, I was staying with my son and his family when they had a get-together with his wife, "Corrine's," father. His wife, Corrine's stepmother, had just finished chemo for several different types of cancer. When Corrine's dad went to leave, I offered to put together a small plate for his wife, hoping it would make her feel better.</p><p>When Corrine saw this from the outside, she came in and accused me of "giving away family food that her son might want." They have lots of money, and I replied that I just thought it would be nice for the recovering woman, and if Corrine thought she needed more food for her son, I'd be happy to get it.</p><p>My son and his wife have barely spoken to me since. I have offered to meet them for counseling and have sent my grandson little gifts every month, which have gone unacknowledged. I saw them for the first time last month at a family wedding. They barely said a word, and my son avoided me. The rest of the family could not believe how rude they were to me.</p><p>I don't know what else to do. I have reached out. I've written notes. When I talk with my son on the phone, he's receptive. Then he talks to his wife, and all of a sudden, nothing is acceptable. Please help. — <i>ESTRANGED IN CALIFORNIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR ESTRANGED:</b> Could there be more behind this than you have mentioned — perhaps hurt feelings that drove Corinne over the edge? You have done all you can to make up with your super-sensitive daughter-in-law (who appears to be uniquely possessive of her food). Take a step back. Sometimes, things get better with time, and that is what I am hoping will happen for you.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> A year ago, I got out of a verbally abusive relationship. Five months later, I met the man of my dreams, who had also been in a very bad marriage. We are really good together, but if something bad happens, he flies off the handle and accuses me of being stupid and not normal. He also threatens to leave me if I don't change my behavior. This was the same threat I got from my ex. I suspect that when I get upset about a problem, he thinks I'm his ex-wife. What should I do? I love him, but I don't want to be back in the same kind of relationship as before. — <i>SCARED AND CONFUSED IN MICHIGAN</i></p><p><b>DEAR SCARED:</b> You may not want to be back in the same kind of relationship that you had before, but it looks like that's almost exactly where you are. I don't blame you for being scared and confused because there is something wrong with your manpicker. You have now been with two emotional abusers. Before involving yourself in any more romantic relationships, it's important that you discuss this with a psychologist or other licensed mental health professional who can help you break this pattern. If you do, you'll spare yourself years of bad choices and heartache.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>Good advice for everyone — teens to seniors — is in "The Anger in All of Us and How to Deal With It." To order, send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds) to: Dear Abby, Anger Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: Girls run the court at Chicago Bulls' annual clinic
entries.summary: <p>White-and-orange WNBA basketballs cut through the air inside the Chicago Bulls training facility Saturday as the squeak of sneakers and the thump of dribbling echoed across the hardwood.</p><p>About 150 girls moved through drills when Beyoncé’s anthem filled the gym: “Who run the world? Girls.”</p><p>The clinic was part of the Chicago Bulls’ and Gatorade’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls/2025/03/05/bulls-host-2nd-annual-girls-day-of-play-for-girls-to-understand-theres-a-place-for-them-in-sports" >third annual</a> Girls’ Day of Play, a Women’s History Month event aimed at introducing basketball to girls aged eight to 18 in an inclusive environment. It also marked the culmination of a six-month coaching initiative that provides 50 Chicago-area coaches with resources to support female-identifying athletes throughout their seasons.</p><p>“We were trying to figure out how we, as a men's professional team, address the rates of girls dropping out or not even joining sports,” said Adrienne Scherenzel, Bulls vice president of community engagement. “We can’t get to all the girls, but we know we can get to the coaches.”</p><p>The coaching development program partners with the nonprofit Center for Healing and Justice Through Sport, along with Bulls youth hoops coaches, to train Chicago-area coaches on how to better encourage, support and develop their athletes.</p><p>Scherenzel said the program is designed to respond to questions coaches have throughout their seasons. For example, some male coaches have asked how to better support athletes during menstrual cycles, prompting the program to provide care packages with menstrual products.</p><p>“It's a nice, discreet, black case, so they can take it with them, and just have it on the bus, or in their first aid kit,” Scherenzel said, “so if girls need products, they can always get them there.”</p><div of here, you'll be like, 10 times more confident, because I definitely was.”</p><p></p><p>Athletes and coaches alike also took note of DJ Hillery Banks, who mixed artists like Olivia Dean and The Cheetah Girls with Chicago house music to keep the energy high. entries.title: Labeled a gang member and deported, longtime Chicagoan tries to restart in his Mexican hometown
entries.summary: <p>Francisco Gonzalez-Jasso, a longtime Little Village resident, didn't know exactly how to make his way back to his childhood home in Torreón, a city in Mexico's northern state of Cahuila. He hadn’t been there in 33 years.</p><p>“I kept asking people on the bus, 'Is Torreón next?' ” Gonzalez-Jasso, 55, says in his native Spanish.</p><p>In Torreón, he took a cab to his old block. But the years had erased his memory of the house. He paced the street, checking the addresses on every door. When he found the right one, he says, the house looked different. It was really small.</p><p>“I started yelling out my brother’s name: Cesar, Cesar,” Gonzalez-Jasso says. “Once I saw his face, I told the taxi driver to leave. Then, I embraced my brother.</p><p>“I was broken.".</p><p>The last time they were together, Cesar, now 50, was 17.</p><p>Gonzalez-Jasso is trying to rebuild his life in Mexico after he was arrested by Border Patrol agents last October in Little Village in front of friends and neighbors. He was deported a few days later. WBEZ has been keeping up with Gonzalez-Jasso after visiting him in Mexico in December, not long after he arrived there.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Gonzalez-Jasso has breakfast at his brother’s house in February. He has a large extended family in his hometown but the adjustment back home has been a struggle.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Duilio Rodríguez/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The tall man with a sturdy build was a well-known presence in his Chicago neighborhood for more than three decades. Still, despite not having a criminal record, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security branded him a member of the Latin Kings gang — a tag that has followed him to Mexico.</p><p>Gonzalez-Jasso is among hundreds of people swept up during Operation Midway Blitz, the aggressive Trump administration deportation campaign aimed at clearing “violent criminals” off Chicago-area streets. He also is among immigrants who say they were wrongly accused of being a criminal or having ties to gangs.</p><p>“It’s humiliating for me,” Gonzalez-Jasso says. “I’m not a criminal. I never harmed anyone.”</p><h3>‘This was his home’ </h3><p>Gonzalez-Jasso was known on 26th Street in Little Village as Panchito. His arrest and deportation last fall were a gut punch to neighbors who remember him as a friendly face always ready to lend a hand.</p><p>“I cried, honestly, I cried when I learned that Panchito was arrested,” Carlos Macías, the owner of Carniceria y Taqueria Aguas Calientes on 26th street, said in Spanish. The two have been friends for more than 20 years.</p><p>Also speaking Spanish, Ana Guerrero, a waitress at the <i>taqueria</i> who often served Gonzalez-Jasso, said: “He was like your daily coffee, always here in the mornings before heading to work. He was always very respectful. This was his home.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-960000" name="image-960000"></a> That's when Border Patrol agents arrested him.</p><p>“The saddest thing, and it hurts, is that they grabbed me, they forced me down, pointed a gun at me, in front of people, children.” Gonzalez-Jasso says. “Your world collapses. He hadn’t slept, showered or changed clothes in days. He was in pain from the punches during his arrest, he says.</p><p>He spent two days in bed. It took him several weeks to feel like himself again, he says.</p><p>“I kept thinking, ‘What am I going to do,’” he says. “I was deported like the worst criminal. My reputation is gone.”</p><p>And the home where he was now living wasn’t what he remembered. Over the years, he had lost both his parents and two brothers. The faded curtains and worn furniture were a constant reminder that three decades had passed, that his parents were no longer there to hold things together.</p><p>Gonzalez-Jasso says he felt like an intruder there despite his brother's efforts to make him feel welcome. Cesar was living there with his wife and three children.</p><p>His brother and other relatives had seen the videos of his arrest even before he arrived — making his integration that much harder. When his sister heard of his arrest, she was so shaken she almost had a nervous breakdown.</p><p>“I didn’t want anyone to know I was thrown out like that,” Gonzalez-Jasso says.</p><div deportation, Gonzalez-Jasso is living on a modest pension from his construction work. He shipped his clothes from Chicago and gave away the furniture he left behind. He is trying to get someone to haul his two cars.</p><p>He’s keeping busy remodeling his parents’ home, doing a complete overhaul of the kitchen and the bedrooms.</p><p>But he worries about the violence in Mexico. One of his brothers disappeared years ago and was never found.</p><p>Once in a while, he replays the video of his arrest. It’s painful to hear the sounds — the whistles, a woman yelling <i>“la migra”</i> — and to see himself surrounded by Border Patrol agents.</p><p>Gonzalez-Jasso wants to clear his name so everyone knows he’s not a gang member. But he doesn’t know where to start.</p><p>And he misses his Little Village friends and neighbors. Some of them recently traveled to Mexico to see him for a few days. They aren't his blood relatives. But they were his family.</p><p>In Chicago, he says, his voice cracking, “There are many people who love me. And I miss them.”</p>

entries.title: Jesse Jackson’s hometown determined to preserve its rich shared history amid rapid change
entries.summary: <p>GREENVILLE, S.C. — Black children in Greenville couldn’t wait to grow up and go to Sterling High School, many graduates recall. Now what remains are memories of its majorettes and its championship sports and its excellent, committed teachers.</p><p>A young Jesse Jackson shone there, as a three-letter athlete who earned a football scholarship, as an activist and as an all-around student. Known to set hearts on campus aflutter, he graced many a page in the 1959 Torch yearbook published by the county’s oldest Black high school.</p><p>On an unofficial tour of “Jesse Jackson” landmarks, there’s not much left to see of the school,<b> </b>which mysteriously<b> </b>burned in 1967.</p><p>There also are few markers to highlight historic integration and civil rights efforts made by Jackson and others that altered Greenville's history, current leaders say, and continue to shape it today.</p><p>Jackson’s home state on Monday granted him a hero’s welcome, acknowledging him as a son of South Carolina. It cordoned off its grand Capitol rotunda for a lying in honor so thousands of<b> </b>ordinary citizens could pay their respects to one of the most influential Americans to come from the Palmetto State. Leola Robinson-Simpson in her Greenville home on March 3. She and Jesse Jackson met as classmates at Greenville’s Sterling High School.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“Jesse had come down, and he was just determined to do some things to make sure that Greenville wasn't the only [county] in the union that hadn't passed the national King holiday, so he was in and out of Greenville all the time,” says Robinson-Simpson, a former South Carolina state representative. Jesse led a mass demonstration of an estimated 30,000 across a bridge, and then a second march down Main Street, she says.</p><p>And nothing stands to honor the Greenville Eight or mark the county<b> </b>library branch where eight NAACP youth council members, including a 19-year-old Jackson home from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. They sat in the well appointed whites-only library to protest segregation’s shoddy conditions at the “colored library” until police were called. Jesse Jackson comes home to South Carolina, the place that molded the man Chicago knew</a> </div> <div class="PagePromo-description">Jackson lay in honor at the South Carolina State Capitol on Monday. His ties to the state and Greenville, his hometown that nurtured him and inspired his activism, always remained strong.</div> <div class="PagePromo-byline"><div class="PagePromo-date"> <bsp-timestamp data-timestamp=1772508717000 data-promo="true"> <template data-date-tpl>[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]</template> <span data-date> </span> </bsp-timestamp><span class="dot"></span></div> <div class="PagePromo-author"> <span>By </span><strong><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/lauren-fitzpatrick" >Lauren FitzPatrick </a></strong>  and  <strong><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/audio-by-somer-van-benton" > Somer Van Benton, audio </a></strong> </div> <div class="PagePromo-readingTime"> <span class="dot-divider"></span> <svg class="PagePromo-readingTime-icon"> <use xlink:href="#icon-clock-reading"></use> </svg> <span class="PagePromo-readingTime-text"> <bsp-time-to-read data-article-word-count="1292"></bsp-time-to-read> read </span> </div> </div> </div> </div> </div> </div> </bsp-list-loadmore><p>At best, the city installed a bronze statue of a pair of Black children outside the former Woolworth’s five-and-dime store where Sterling High School students, including some of the Greenville Eight, staged sit-ins at lunch counters and picketed. Ultimately a 1963 Supreme Court decision struck down such segregation.</p><p>Rev. Stacy Mills, the pastor of Mountain View Baptist Church, is tasked with leading the city’s efforts for a monument. He called the “best tribute to Rev. Jackson” a concrete commitment to economic security for everyone in Greenville.</p><p>“So we are required to dedicate ourselves to economic equality in deed, not word,” Mills says, “and a commitment to a tangible memorial to the work of this Greenvillian born and forged in this community whose work is felt around the world.”</p><p>What that memorial will look like or where it should go remains to be seen. Greenville Mayor Knox White says that meetings with key people were first held more than a year ago and city staff have been assigned to support such a project.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-de0000" name="image-de0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e31fc34/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fab%2Fe9%2Fa718ae734178bc3ec373582a983f%2Fjjsouthcarolina-260303-42.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b15ba15/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fab%2Fe9%2Fa718ae734178bc3ec373582a983f%2Fjjsouthcarolina-260303-42.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5e22aad/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fab%2Fe9%2Fa718ae734178bc3ec373582a983f%2Fjjsouthcarolina-260303-42.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Greenville Mayor Knox White speaks during a private service for the Rev. Jesse Jackson as he lays in honor inside the South Carolina Capitol." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5e22aad/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fab%2Fe9%2Fa718ae734178bc3ec373582a983f%2Fjjsouthcarolina-260303-42.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ebf313f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fab%2Fe9%2Fa718ae734178bc3ec373582a983f%2Fjjsouthcarolina-260303-42.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5e22aad/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fab%2Fe9%2Fa718ae734178bc3ec373582a983f%2Fjjsouthcarolina-260303-42.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Greenville Mayor Knox White speaks during a private service for the Rev. Jesse Jackson inside the South Carolina Capitol on March 2.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“Rev. J and I always discussed ways in which he’d be honored,” White says. “He was grateful. Lots of private citizens have long expressed willingness to help.</p><p>“The city is full of commemorative art, including to civil rights-era themes and people. There has never been much question about Rev Jackson’s legacy being a part of that.”</p><p>At the private Capitol ceremony for Jackson in Columbia, White used his remarks to thank Jackson for helping to modernize and reinvigorate Greenville, long ago booming with textile mills, by insisting on desegregation.</p><p>“By tearing down the walls of segregation, Rev. Jackson and other courageous leaders also blazed a new path of freedom for the people of South Carolina and allowed our state to become the place it is today,” White told Jackson’s relatives and the invited dignitaries. “As he would remind us in more recent times, it is unimaginable that a BMW or a Boeing would locate in a segregated South Carolina. Of course not. He freed us all.”<br></p>

entries.title: No one injured after Morton Grove condo floor collapses
entries.summary: <p>The floor of a Morton Grove condo partially collapsed Saturday night, according to the Morton Grove Police Department.</p><p>The collapse happened around 8 p.m. in a second-floor unit in the building at 5935 Lincoln Avenue. The condo building was fully evacuated and no injuries were reported, police said.</p><p>The building will remain closed until it’s found to be structurally sound.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Two men shot during fight at 79th St Red Line station
entries.summary: <p>Two men were shot after a fight broke out at the 79th Street CTA Red Line station early Sunday, Chicago police said.</p><p>An argument led to the fight and involved “several” people around 1 a.m. Sunday, according to police.</p><p>A 21-year-old man was shot in the chest, and a 23-year-old man was shot in the buttocks. Both were taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center in serious condition.</p><p>Three males were arrested and two guns were recovered, police said.</p><p>Red Line trains bypassed the station for over two hours and resumed stops at 79th Street around 4:45 a.m. Sunday, according to CTA alerts.<br></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Two women fatally shot in Washington Heights
entries.summary: <p>Two women were fatally shot in the far South Side Washington Heights neighborhood Saturday night, Chicago police said.</p><p>Officers found the women — 68-year-old Phyllis Goolsby and a 71-year-old woman — fatally shot in the chest in the 10400 block of South Peoria Street before 11 p.m., according to the Cook County medical examiner's office and police. They were both pronounced dead at the scene. The 71-year-old woman's name has not been released.</p><p>A 75-year-old man was arrested at the scene and taken into custody. A weapon was recovered.<br></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Sectional rewind: Breaking down Friday's IHSA state tournament action
entries.summary: <p>There was some chatter when the season began about several teams that would be making the jump from Class 3A to 4A.</p><p>The discussion centered mostly on how much stronger the state’s largest class would become with the additions of DePaul Prep, Mount Carmel, St. Patrick and a few others. But while the strength in numbers is certainly true in the 4A conversation, there were also some questions among basketball junkies of just how might it play out for those respective teams in the largest class?</p><p>While playing the regular season in what has now become the state’s toughest conference, the Chicago Catholic League, and putting together tough, class-proof non-conference schedules, DePaul Prep and St. Ignatius have built their strong, respected reputations in a multitude of ways.</p><p>However, regardless of a school’s enrollment, there is no denying thriving in the postseason in Class 2A and 3A is different than in Class 4A. And in recent years both DePaul and Ignatius have propped up their programs in impressive fashion with state tournament runs in smaller classes.</p><p>DePaul has been building a treasure trove of state basketball trophies in the trophy case. It started with a third-place finish in Class 3A in 2019, followed by a third-place finish in Class 2A in 2022.</p><p>Then three straight state championships followed over the past three years, winning a Class 2A title in 2023 and then a pair of 3A titles in 2024 and 2025.</p><p>St. Ignatius, meanwhile, won just its second sectional title in program history in 2022. The Wolfpack followed it up with another one the next year. Both seasons ended in Champaign with third and fourth-place finishes in Class 3A.</p><p>Now? Both DePaul and St. Ignatius are one win away from securing another state trophy — this time in Class 4A. And they did so by winning two of the toughest Class 4A sectionals in the state.</p><p>“They knew the stakes were higher and that it would be tougher,” DePaul coach Tom Kleinschmidt said of his team’s mentality of playing in a 4A sectional.</p><p>It didn’t matter. DePaul headed to the North Shore where Evanston and New Trier have won six of the last seven sectionals that have been played. The Rams beat them both in the sectional.</p><p>Due to who DePaul was playing, Kleinschmidt felt he maybe had the attention of his players a bit more in the lead up.</p><p>“Our kids seemed more focused in practice and in our prep for these games,” Kleinschmidt said. “They were locked in. They knew who they were playing — very good, ranked teams with kids they knew, have played against and are aware of from New Trier and Evanston.”</p><p>St. Ignatius just swept through the Chicago Public League, beating Kenwood, Simeon and Curie in succession to win its third sectional title in five years. Coach Matt Monroe called the stretch a “gauntlet” in discussing the road to a 4A sectional title.</p><p>Monroe admits it’s a bit dissimilar to DePaul because the Wolfpack were a 4A school last season. But he did say everything felt different in winning a 4A sectional.</p><p>“It does feel like a bigger deal,” Monroe said in regard to winning a 4A sectional compared to past 3A titles.</p><p>St. Ignatius has played Simeon four times in the last five years. The first two were as 3A schools, matching up in the IHSA State Finals in Champaign. Last year and this season the two tangled much earlier — in a regional last year and in this past week’s sectional.</p><p>“Our regional championship against Kenwood felt more like a sectional game,” Monroe pointed out. “And our sectional championship game against Curie felt more like a downstate, Final Four game. So, yes, I do think it felt bigger for our guys.”</p><p>➤ Kaneland is super again.</p><p>The undefeated Knights will play in their second straight super-sectional on Monday. Only this time they’ll be playing in their back yard, looking to improve to 34-0 on the year.</p><p>A year ago when Kaneland won its first sectional title in 43 years, the Knights traveled to the Hoffman Estates Super where they were pummeled by eventual state champ DePaul Prep.</p><p>This year they play in the DeKalb Super, just a 14-mile trip for Kaneland and its fans.</p><p>➤ Marist and Kankakee entered Friday night in similar positions.</p><p>Both were looking to end decades-long sectional droughts. For Marist it’s been 45 years, while Kankakee’s last sectional title came in 1960.</p><p>And both were regarded as arguably the best teams in school history, which added a sense of urgency as they took the floor for their respective sectional championship games.</p><p>While Marist marches on to a super-sectional date with Peoria Richwoods, Kankakee’s dream season — and the high school career of star Lincoln Williams — comes to a screeching halt.</p><p>Kankakee jumped out to a quick 9-0 lead over red-hot Morton, which has now ripped off 22 straight wins, but couldn’t hold on. The Kays fell 61-48 in the Ottawa Sectional final.</p><p>➤ What a season it’s been for Charles Barnes. He’s led Marist to 30 wins and a sectional title while averaging 18 points a game. The 6-5 senior who transferred in for his senior season has been brilliant for the RedHawks all season, including a game-high 31 points in the sectional title win over Homewood-Flossmoor.</p><p>But the athletically-gifted 6-7 Stephen Brown has helped take the RedHawks to another level during this postseason push.</p><p>An up-and-down basketball career, which has included early hype, injuries, juggling time between football and basketball and then an inconsistent senior year, is all in the rearview mirror. The North Carolina State football recruit has been a revelation. His higher engagement level and buy-in has led to greater production.</p><p>Brown put up a double-double in the regional win over Rich and another one in the sectional semifinal victory over Lockport with 18 points and 13 rebounds. Then in the 55-49 win over H-F to win the sectional, Brown chipped 14 points and seven rebounds.</p><p>➤ York scored 12 points in the second half of the sectional championship game. It didn’t matter. The Dukes still won, beating high-scoring Glenbard East 37-36. Remember, this was a Glenbard East team that had scored 60-plus points 26 times this season.</p><p>But York’s bread and butter remains the same no matter who it plays or what part of the season: defense.</p><p>The Dukes play with size and physicality — and just enough scoring to go with it — but it’s the ball press zone defense that former coach Vince Doran implemented in 2014 that has been difference-making. As a result, the Dukes claimed their first sectional championship in 1982.</p><p>Throw in a school record 31 wins, and it’s been an amazing season for coach Mike Dunn’s Dukes.</p><p>But it starts with the ball press, which Dunn continued upon taking over the program in 2020. Dunn had only played man-to-man as a head coach with Yorkville.</p><p>“I had never played a possession of zone as a head coach,” Dunn admits.</p><p>Dunn, the student, sat down with Doran, the teacher, and it began. Dunn then went and talked to several coaches who were playing the ball press, including Mike Healy at Wheaton South, Eric Millstone at Palatine and recently retired coaches Paul Harris at Highland Park and Mike Miller at Rockton-Hononegah.</p><p>“We decided to stick with it and it’s been really good,” Dunn said. “JJ Pearl, my assistant, is fantastic with it and the reason we are so good at it.”</p><p>The ball press has been a neutralizer, limiting foes to less than 50 points all season and to just 36 points a game in York’s last 11 wins.</p><p>➤ As ranked teams all season while marching through sectional play, DePaul Prep and St. Ignatius have hogged up a lot of headlines among Chicago Catholic League teams. But less-talked-about Leo and St. Francis are also on the doorstep of reaching the IHSA State Finals in Class 3A.</p><p>Could the Chicago Catholic League make up half of the 3A and 4A field next weekend in Champaign?</p><p>As a No. 7 sectional seed, St. Francis is the lowest-seeded team still playing. In fact, the remaining 3A field of eight teams consists of six No. 1 seeds, one No. 2 seed and seventh-seeded St. Francis.</p><p>The Spartans have lived on the edge this postseason. That continued with an overtime thriller over Wheaton Academy. They will face Deerfield in the Hoffman Estates Super.</p><p>Coach Jimalle Ridley’s Leo program, which won the Catholic League White, has been knocking on the door in each of the past two seasons. Leo won regional titles in 2024 and 2025, including last year’s heartbreaking 44-43 loss in the sectional final to Dyett.</p><p>➤ How about some Red-West flavor spicing up the smaller classes?</p><p>While they aren’t the powers they once were from back in the day, former West Side powers Farragut, Crane and Marshall are all still alive in state tournament play. All three will play in Joliet on Monday night.</p><p>Farragut and Crane will meet with a trip to Champaign on the line in Class 2A, while Marshall will play in a Class 1A super-sectional, facing Indian Creek.</p><p>➤ If you’ve been reading these pages or listening to the No Shot Clock podcast in recent weeks, you’ve heard superlatives being thrown around about Peoria Richwoods sophomore Amarion Smith-Holley. He’s become this year’s Mr. March.</p><p>The 5-11 point guard went for 31 in a sizzling regional championship game performance against Rock Island. He scored 29, including three game-winning free throws with no time on the clock, to beat Normal 68-67 in the sectional semis.</p><p>Smith-Holley scored 21 more in a 59-58 win over Edwardsville, once again adding to his growing reputation as an ultra-clutch player. His late steal led to being fouled and knocking down the two game-winning free throws with 12 seconds to play.</p><p>Smith-Holley is now one win away from showcasing himself as one of the state’s elite talents on the state’s biggest stage.</p>

entries.title: Man fatally shot in North Lawndale home
entries.summary: <p>A 25-year-old man was fatally shot Sunday morning in a North Lawndale home, Chicago police said.</p><p>The man was arguing with another person at the home in the 2100 block of South Trumbull Avenue when the person pulled out a gun and shot the man three times in the chest about 8 a.m., according to police.</p><p>He was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital where he was pronounced dead. No one has been arrested, according to police.</p>

entries.title: Michael O'Brien's Super 25 high school basketball rankings for March 8, 2026
entries.summary: <p>Four of the eight Class 4A sectional finals on Friday featured private schools against public schools. The private schools swept, with Benet, DePaul Prep, Marist and St. Ignatius all picking up wins.</p><p>All four schools will be favored in the supersectionals on Monday, so there is a strong possibility the Class 4A field in Champaign will be all private schools.</p><p>So far, there is no uproar from high school sports fans. The basketball landscape is different from football. Public high schools have dominated Illinois high school basketball since the state tournament began in 1908.</p><p>Benet’s Class 4A championship last season was the first big-school title won by a private school since St. Joseph’s AA title in 1999.</p><p>DePaul Prep, Benet and St. Ignatius have been regulars in the state semifinals for the past several years. Marist has never advanced to state before. The RedHawks lost to Proviso East in the supersectionals in 1981.</p><p>Five private schools advanced to supersectionals in the smaller classes. Leo and St. Francis are still alive in 3A, McNamara and Quincy Notre Dame in 2A and Routt in 1A.</p><p>These may be the glory years for private schools in Illinois high school basketball. How successful will they be? How long will it last? That’s all still to be seen. The Public League won every Class 4A state title but one from 2009 through 2017. Only Jalen Brunson’s Stevenson team in 2015 broke the CPS stranglehold.</p><h3>Public League Champaign dreams</h3><p>Curie’s loss to St. Ignatius eliminated CPS from Class 4A, but the Public League is very much alive in the state playoffs overall.</p><p>Hyde Park will face Leo in the Class 3A UIC supersectional on Monday. Crane and Farragut will face off in the Class 2A Joliet Central supersectional and Marshall takes on Indian Creek in the Class 1A Joliet Central supersectional.</p><p>The Cougars, led by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-basketball/2026/02/20/chicago-sun-times-all-city-high-school-basketball-team-2026" >All-City selections</a> Brad Blackmon and Jamier Montgomery, are legitimate contenders to win Class 2A.</p><h3>Star watching</h3><p>The three biggest stars in the area next year will be Warren’s Jaxson Davis, Neuqua Valley’s Cole Kelly and Brady Pettigrew of Bolingbrook.</p><p>It’s still early, but right now from what I’m hearing, all three players will return to their high schools next year and not head to prep schools. Obviously, things can change over the next few months, but there seems to be a solid chance the area will hold on to its star power.</p><p>Davis said last week that he has no reason to leave. Kelly has referenced next year at Neuqua Valley several times in interviews and Pettigrew’s father, Titcus, is the head football coach at Bolingbrook and said on Friday that he “isn’t interested in the prep school thing.”</p><p>Keeping all three players in the state would be huge for Illinois high school basketball. And for anyone starting to get worked up about the public vs. private issue, it is worth noting that all three stars are at public schools.</p><p><b>Super 25 high school basketball rankings for March 8, 2026</b><br>With record and last week's ranking</p><p><b>1.
